clue.text: Supports — ticks

definitions.meaning: to second a motion is to back it, which is what a supporter at a meeting does
each tick of a clock marks off one unit of time, sixty of them to the minute

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the whole disguise: two unrelated senses of one word sit either side of it, one from the committee room and one from the clock face.
explanation.definitionFit: Supports backs a motion the way a seconder does; ticks are the clock's own units — one word, two everyday senses.

clue.text: Red insect with horn's noise entertaining King

parts.note: the three-letter insect a setter reaches for first

indicators.note: To entertain a guest is to have them in your house, so the word that entertains holds the other letter inside itself.

parts.note: the noise a horn makes, written the way comics spell it
R is the crossword king, from the Latin Rex stamped on coins and documents

explanation.walkthrough: The insect and the horn belong to a garden afternoon, and 'entertaining King' sounds like a royal visit — nothing in the surface admits that a colour is being built.
explanation.definitionFit: Red: the deep purple-red of the vegetable is a colour in its own right, the shade a blushing face is said to go.

clue.text: Lapel splotched with a saffrony mixture

indicators.note: splotched with means blotched and mixed in with, so the letters of lapel and a are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A diner's mishap: a jacket lapel stained with a yellow, saffron-coloured dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splotched' scatters the letters of LAPEL and A. 'saffrony mixture' looks like a description of the stain, but it defines the Spanish rice dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is a Spanish dish of rice cooked with seafood or meat and flavoured and coloured with saffron.

clue.text: A little prude can't eradicate provider of vino

indicators.note: Asking for a little of a phrase is asking for a short piece of the letters themselves, not for a word that means something smaller.

parts.note: eight letters run without a break from the end of the first word, through the whole of the second and into the third; the apostrophe is no obstacle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't eradicate' reads as a stubborn stain and the prude as the person complaining about it. The three words are only a letter run.
explanation.definitionFit: provider of vino: the glass jug wine is poured into and served out of at table, so it is what supplies your glass.

clue.text: 'Lavish' starter for lunch covered in young insects sent back

indicators.note: A starter is the first thing to arrive, so what is taken from the word after it is the letter it begins with.
Something sent back retraces the way it came, so those letters are written out in the opposite order.
To be covered in something is to have it all round you, so the letter ends up inside the other piece rather than beside it.

parts.note: a pupa is an insect at its second stage, between grub and adult
the opening letter of the meal, and nothing else of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' pulls double duty: on the surface it is the first course of the lavish meal, in the wordplay the first letter of the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Lavish': a slap-up meal is a generous, no-expense-spared spread — British informal, and lavish is precisely the sense meant.

clue.text: Rotten luck, Ken: a horrible kind of 'sandwich'

indicators.note: rotten means decayed and fallen apart, so these letters break down and re-form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Commiserating with Ken over his bad luck with a nasty sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' rearranges the letters of LUCK and KEN. The definition is in quotes because this sandwich is a punch in the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A knuckle sandwich is slang for a punch to the face, an unpleasant thing to be given.

clue.text: Almond cake consumed in Jarbidge, Nevada

indicators.note: What has been consumed has been swallowed whole by what surrounds it, so the letters sit unbroken inside the words that follow.

parts.note: six letters run straight on from the end of the town's name into the start of the state's, comma and all

explanation.walkthrough: Jarbidge is a real Nevada town, and it is in the clue for one reason: its last two letters and the state's first four sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Almond cake: a Geneva cake is the dense French bake made with ground almonds in place of flour, so a city's name doubles as a recipe.

clue.text: Vino — cheese (not started) — then cocktail

parts.note: brie is the cheese, and lopping off the letter it opens with leaves three
a sling is a long mixed drink — gin sling, Singapore sling

explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make the clue look like three items on a wine list. Only the middle one is a word to be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Vino: a German white grape and the wine pressed from it, so the slangy word for wine defines the answer by kind.

clue.text: Pungent ingredient presenting unfortunate gastric ordeal

indicators.note: unfortunate suggests things gone wrong, so these letters come out in a disordered state

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A strong-smelling ingredient leads to an upset stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunate' rearranges all thirteen letters of GASTRIC ORDEAL. The surface's indigestion fits a cooking ingredient.
explanation.definitionFit: Garlic cooked in the oven is a strongly flavoured ingredient in many dishes.

clue.text: Everything I left over? An omelette and a cake

indicators.note: Something turned over ends up facing the way it came from, so the assembled pieces are read out from their far end.

parts.note: the everyday word for the whole of something
the pronoun is taken at face value, as the single letter it is written with
a Trot is a Trotskyist, British shorthand for someone well over on the political left

explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the turning instruction an across clue would use; it is a person instead, and the little word after it does the turning.
explanation.definitionFit: An omelette and a cake: a Spanish tortilla is a potato omelette, a Mexican one a flat maize cake — one word, both dishes.

clue.text: A small image's showing jellies

parts.note: the clue's own first word, taken as the letter it is
S for small, as on a clothing label
a pic is a picture, the short form used in every newspaper office
the apostrophe-s reads as a possessive on the surface and hands over a letter in the wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is fond of letting an apostrophe-s do a letter's work; here it is the S that makes the answer plural, which the enumeration never warns you about.
explanation.definitionFit: jellies: savoury meat or vegetable jellies set clear in a mould, so the plural noun swaps straight in.

clue.text: Champion mostly having swallowed a liqueur

indicators.note: What swallows a thing takes it right inside, so the letter goes into the middle of the word rather than after it.

parts.note: to champion a cause is to advocate it; docked of its last letter that leaves seven
the article is swallowed whole, as the single letter it is written with

explanation.walkthrough: Wordplay and drink share a root: advocaat is Dutch for a lawyer, and the thick egg-and-brandy drink was reckoned good for a pleader's throat.
explanation.definitionFit: liqueur: the thick, sweet Dutch egg-yolk-and-brandy drink is one of the sweetened spirits that word covers.

clue.text: Before curt excuse, spill drink

indicators.note: Putting one piece before another places it in front, so what the clue mentions second is written first.

parts.note: to tip a bucket over is to spill what is in it
a plea is an excuse, shortened here by a letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has someone apologising and knocking a glass over. Read as instructions it is the excuse that gets cut short, not the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: drink: your tipple is the drink you habitually take — 'what's your tipple?' — an everyday, slightly jocular noun.

clue.text: Drunk at Conference perhaps suggesting compote

indicators.note: at means next to, so the first piece sits right beside the second

parts.note: stewed is slang for drunk
Conference is a variety of pear, an example of fruit

explanation.surface: Someone drunk at a conference has a suggestive word to say about dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conference' looks like a meeting, but it is a well-known pear variety in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A compote is a dessert of fruit cooked slowly in syrup, which is fruit that has been stewed.

clue.text: Catch intro to elegant music where one may drink elegantly

parts.note: to catch a prize is to win it

indicators.note: An intro is the opening of a thing, so what is taken from the word after it is the letter it starts with.

parts.note: the first letter of the word, and no more of it
written music is divided into bars

explanation.walkthrough: The word 'elegant' works twice over: once to give up its opening letter, and once, as an adverb, to say what sort of drinking place is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: where one may drink elegantly: these sell wine by the glass in more genteel surroundings than a pub, so the phrase names them by function.

clue.text: Dessert: the writer emits shrill laugh audibly

indicators.note: audibly says the phrase is spoken aloud and heard as another

parts.note: the writer is the setter, I, and emitting a shrill laugh is to scream, so the phrase is I SCREAM

explanation.surface: A dessert prompts the setter to let out a shrill laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: The playground rhyme 'I scream, you scream, we all scream for ice cream' plays on the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is a frozen sweet made from cream or milk, served as a pudding after a meal.

clue.text: Every so often, Linus boils angrily — being this?

definitions.note: The definition is a pointer rather than a synonym: 'this' is the state the clue has just painted — someone boiling with anger — and BILIOUS is the adjective for it.

indicators.note: Doing a thing angrily is doing it wildly and with no care for order, so the letters land out of their proper places.
Something done every so often is done at regular intervals, and the letters are taken at intervals too — every second one.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the name, picked out in turn
all five letters go into the mix, to be re-sorted along with the two above

explanation.walkthrough: 'Boils angrily' looks like the definition and is really fodder plus its instruction. The definition is the two words after the dash, pointing back at the whole picture.
explanation.definitionFit: being this?: the clue points at its own scene — bilious means liverish and bad-tempered, which is what a man boiling with anger is.

clue.text: 'Unfinished, Cubistic' — confused, perhaps — snap!

definitions.note: a snap is a crisp biscuit, as in a ginger snap; perhaps marks it as an example

indicators.note: confused means muddled, so the remaining letters are jumbled
unfinished drops the final letter of the word

parts.note: the art-style adjective supplies the letters

explanation.surface: An art critic's verdict on an unfinished Cubist painting: confused, perhaps, and snapped out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished' drops the last C of CUBISTIC; 'confused' jumbles CUBISTI. 'snap!' reads as an exclamation, but a snap, like a ginger snap, is a crisp biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A ginger snap is a thin brittle cookie, so a snap is one kind of the answer.

clue.text: Home, once more begins to eat

parts.note: digs are lodgings — the British word for rented rooms you go home to
the words ask for home a second time, and someone who is in is at home

explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'Home, once more' read as a weary arrival, when it is really an instruction to give a word for home twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: begins to eat: to dig in is to set about a meal with appetite — 'dig in!' is the invitation at the table — and the tense matches.

clue.text: Plans sent back: Everyman's persistently irritating online

indicators.note: Something sent back travels the way it came, so the letters of the word before it are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: plans in the draughtsman's sense — street plans are maps
the setter signs himself Everyman, so his own possessive is these two letters

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman writes himself into his own wordplay: whenever this puzzle says 'Everyman's', it means 'my'. Worth remembering — he does it most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: persistently irritating online: spammy describes the junk that keeps arriving unasked in an inbox, which is exactly that nuisance.

clue.text: Yankiness yardstick?

definitions.meaning: the invented noun asks what makes a thing American, which sends you hunting for a flag, a president or a state
a yardstick is what other things are measured against, and the phrase wanted is the one Americans use for something that could not be more American

explanation.walkthrough: 'As American as apple pie' is the set phrase, so the yardstick turns out to be a pudding. There is no wordplay here to find — the whole clue is one definition, told slant.
explanation.definitionFit: Yankiness yardstick?: the simile 'as American as apple pie' makes the pudding the standard measure of Americanness, which is a yardstick's job.

clue.text: Gutted: canapés — mixed nuts

indicators.note: mixed means stirred together, so the remaining letters are rearranged
gutted means the insides are taken out, so the central letter of the word goes

parts.note: the letters of canapés, without the accent

explanation.surface: A host devastated that the party snacks are just a bowl of mixed nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' takes the middle letter, the second A, out of CANAPES, leaving CANPES, which 'mixed' rearranges. 'Gutted' reads as British slang for bitterly disappointed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pecans are the edible nuts of the pecan tree, a North American hickory.

clue.text: Baking powder composed of bismuth, calcium and rubidium

parts.note: Bi is the chemical symbol for the element
Ca is the chemical symbol for the element
Rb is the chemical symbol for the element

explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed of' is doing double work: a compound is composed of elements, and so is this answer — three symbols off the periodic table, in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Baking powder: bicarb is bicarbonate of soda, the raising agent sold as baking soda and the working half of baking powder.

clue.text: Sweet bits of lardons in coulis on arborio, perhaps

indicators.note: bits of takes a small piece, the first letter, from each of the following words

parts.note: the four words supply their initial letters
arborio is a variety of rice, used for risotto; perhaps marks it as an example

explanation.surface: An odd recipe: lardons and coulis spooned onto arborio rice, a sweet-and-savoury mix.
explanation.walkthrough: The cooking words are just letter sources: each word after 'bits of' gives its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Licorice is a black confection flavoured with the root of the liquorice plant, a chewy sweet.

clue.text: New recruit, Miles, gets curry powder

indicators.note: A new arrangement is the old one broken up and set out differently, which is what these letters are put through.

parts.note: all seven letters of the word go into the mix as they stand
M is the standard abbreviation for miles, as on a road sign

explanation.walkthrough: Miles is a man on the surface and a unit of distance in the wordplay; the two commas are what make him look like a person being introduced.
explanation.definitionFit: curry powder: turmeric is the yellow ground root that colours the blend, so the setter defines it by the mixture it goes into.

clue.text: Necessity in alimentation; compound; indispensable nutrient, primarily!

definitions.text: Necessity in alimentation; compound; indispensable nutrient, primarily!

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so what each word in the run hands over is the letter it starts with.

parts.words: Necessity in alimentation; compound; indispensable nutrient
parts.note: six words, six opening letters, read straight off in the order they are written

explanation.walkthrough: Every word is doing both jobs at once: read as a sentence the clue describes the vitamin, and read as an instruction each word gives up its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: niacin is vitamin B3, an essential compound the body cannot make and has to take from food.
